title: BYOL
text:
Welcome to BYOL
Building an operating system distribution is one of the most intellectually rewarding journeys in computer systems engineering. Most developers interact with Linux through curated abstractions: package managers like apt or pacman, container runtimes like Docker, or system services managed by systemctl. While these tools offer immense productivity, they often obscure the foundational machinery that powers the platform:

How does the CPU transition from firmware (UEFI) through the bootloader into a running kernel?
What separates a working system from a catastrophic kernel panic during early userspace?
How does a C standard library like glibc or musl interact with kernel system calls?
How do dependency solvers mathematically resolve conflicts across thousands of packages?
What exact sequence transforms a tree of compiled binaries into an ISO image that boots on physical silicon?

BYOL (Build Your Own Linux) lifts the hood. It treats Linux not as a static appliance, but as an orchestrated synthesis of independent open-source subsystems: the Linux kernel, the C runtime, core utility suites, init systems, package managers, network stacks, desktop protocols, and cryptographic trust chains.

title: BYOL
text:
The Trajectory of This Book
This curriculum spans 13 rigorous chapters and a comprehensive Capstone Project, divided into logical engineering phases:

Foundations & Architecture (Chapters 1–2): Explore what truly defines a distribution, deconstruct the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS) and its modern variants (e.g., usr-merge, immutable root filesystems), dissect the monolithic Linux kernel architecture, and master the .config workflow.
The Toolchain & Boot Stack (Chapters 3–4): Build a cross-compilation compiler stack from scratch (binutils, GCC/Clang, glibc vs. musl) using a two-pass bootstrap, trace the boot sequence from reset vector to login prompt, configure bootloaders (GRUB, systemd-boot), and construct custom early-userspace initramfs archives.
Userspace Initialization & Packaging (Chapters 5–7): Implement and compare modern init systems (systemd, OpenRC, s6, runit, BusyBox), design custom package formats and binary repositories, analyze dependency graph SAT-solving algorithms, and establish reproducible build pipelines.
User Experience, Security & Mastering (Chapters 8–10): Stand up modern display stacks (X11 vs. Wayland compositor architecture), harden the system with Linux namespaces, cgroups, SELinux/AppArmor, LUKS full-disk encryption, nftables, and eBPF, and master bootable hybrid ISOs using xorriso and SquashFS.
Infrastructure & Release Engineering (Chapters 11–12): Deploy automated containerized build environments (systemd-nspawn, Docker), examine carrier-grade build networks (Debian buildd, Fedora Koji), establish rolling vs. LTS release policies, and manage CVE backporting workflows.
The Capstone Project (Chapter 13): Integrate every component into an end-to-end production distribution: build the toolchain, cross-compile the kernel, assemble the rootfs, package essential utilities, configure the bootloader, generate a bootable ISO, and verify execution inside QEMU/KVM virtualized test harnesses.

title: BYOL
text:
Who This Book Is For

Systems Engineers & Platform Architects: Professionals looking to master the Linux userspace and kernel boundaries to build customized appliances, embedded systems, edge gateways, or specialized container bases.
Security Researchers & Hardening Specialists: Engineers tasked with building minimal attack-surface operating environments, verifiable supply chains, or tamper-proof appliances.
DevOps, SRE, & Infrastructure Engineers: Technologists who want to understand the mechanics underlying container engines, base images, boot sequences, and distribution packaging.
Curious Programmers: Any developer eager to master Linux at the deepest level by creating an operating system from source code.

A host Linux environment (Debian/Ubuntu, Arch Linux, or Fedora on x86_64 or aarch64).

title: What “From Scratch” Really Means
text:
What “From Scratch” Really Means
The phrase “building Linux from scratch” is frequently invoked in systems engineering, but its definition varies wildly depending on who you ask. To a software developer, it might mean running debootstrap to assemble a custom root filesystem inside a container. To an embedded developer, it might mean running Yocto or Buildroot to cross-compile a board support package. To a purist, it means starting with raw C source code and a C compiler, compiling every binary link by link.
In this book, building a custom Linux operating system from scratch means taking full responsibility for the architectural stack:

title: What “From Scratch” Really Means
text:
The Spectrum of “Custom Distribution”
Distributions exist along a spectrum of autonomy and composition:

Remastered Derivatives: Systems like Linux Mint or Pop!_OS build directly upon Ubuntu’s or Debian’s package repositories. They supply custom desktop environments, installer scripts, and kernel patches, but inherit the upstream packaging infrastructure, ABI, and base system.
Meta-Distributions and Build Systems: Frameworks like Buildroot, Yocto Project (Poky), and Gentoo Linux provide declarative recipes. They automate the compilation of an entire OS image from source, but enforce their own build paradigms and tooling constraints.
Independent Distributions: Distributions like Debian, Arch Linux, Alpine Linux, Void Linux, and Slackware maintain independent packaging formats, build farms, package repositories, and init configurations. They define their own userland conventions and system policies.

In BYOL, we aim for the third tier. You will not simply re-skin an existing live ISO. You will construct: - An isolated cross-toolchain free of host system contamination. - A customized Linux kernel compiled directly from the upstream kernel.org tree. - A chosen C library runtime (glibc or musl). - A functional init system and userspace service manager. - A custom packaging format, repository metadata index, and dependency resolver. - An automated build pipeline and bootable installation ISO image.

title: What “From Scratch” Really Means
text:
The Chicken-and-Egg Problem of Bootstrapping
Every compiled binary needs a compiler. But how do you compile the compiler?
If you compile GCC on your host Ubuntu workstation using /usr/bin/gcc, the resulting compiler may embed hardcoded assumptions, default include search paths (/usr/include), and dynamic loader links (/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2) that point directly back into the host system. If you take that newly compiled GCC and place it onto a clean disk, it will break as soon as it looks for libraries in paths that only existed on the host.
True “from scratch” engineering requires solving this bootstrap problem through a two-pass cross-compilation pipeline: - Pass 1: Build a cross-toolchain that runs on the host but targets a clean, isolated sysroot directory. - Pass 2: Use the cross-toolchain inside the sysroot to compile native tools that only link against the clean target runtime libraries.
Understanding this chain of custody is the essence of building from scratch.

title: Who Should Build a Distribution?
text:
Who Should Build a Distribution?
Building an operating system distribution from source requires patience, technical rigor, and a willingness to confront cryptic compiler errors, linker mismatches, and kernel panic logs. Why do engineers embark on this journey?

title: Who Should Build a Distribution?
text:
1. Engineers Seeking Deep Mastery
Modern software development often abstracts the operating system into a thin configuration file: FROM alpine:latest or image: ubuntu-24.04. When things work, this abstraction is magical. When systems fail under high concurrency, storage latency, or missing shared object dependencies, high-level abstractions break down.
Building a distribution demystifies every layer of Linux: - You discover how dynamic linkers (ld.so) locate shared libraries via DT_RPATH, DT_RUNPATH, and /etc/ld.so.cache. - You learn how the kernel hands control over to process ID 1 (init) and what happens if /dev/console is missing. - You understand how signals, process groups, and process reaping prevent zombie accumulation. - You observe how systemd targets, OpenRC runlevels, or runit supervisory trees establish the user environment.

title: Who Should Build a Distribution?
text:
2. Specialized Platforms and Appliances
General-purpose distributions like Ubuntu and Fedora cater to everyone: desktop users, cloud VMs, gamers, scientists, and enterprise servers. Consequently, they bundle thousands of background services, PAM modules, network helpers, and legacy fallback configurations.
In modern infrastructure, specialized appliances demand radical simplicity: - Kubernetes Node OSs: Modern container-optimized operating systems (e.g., Talos Linux, Flatcar Container Linux, Bottlerocket) remove shells, package managers, and SSH daemons entirely, exposing only an immutable kernel, container runtime, and API endpoint. - Embedded & Edge Systems: Automotive dashboards, network routers, robotics, and industrial controllers require deterministic boot times (under 500 milliseconds), zero unnecessary daemons, and read-only flash storage layouts. - High-Security Enclaves: Financial backends and cryptographic hardware modules require custom kernels with disabled loadable module support (CONFIG_MODULES=n), stripped syscall interfaces, and strict memory sanitization.

title: Who Should Build a Distribution?
text:
3. Supply Chain Security and Reproducibility
When you run apt-get install or dnf install, you are trusting a third-party signing key, upstream build infrastructure, and distribution maintainers. For defense, aerospace, and high-assurance computing, organizations must establish a completely sovereign, verifiable software supply chain.
By mastering the distribution pipeline, you gain the ability to enforce: - Hermetic Build Isolation: Compiling every package inside isolated namespaces without network access. - Deterministic Artifacts: Bit-for-bit identical binaries across independent build machines. - Software Bill of Materials (SBOM): Exact cryptographic tracking of every line of source code, patch, and build flag that enters the final ISO.
Whether your goal is intellectual mastery or building the next generation of infrastructure operating systems, BYOL provides the roadmap.

title: How to Read This Book
text:
How to Read This Book
Building an operating system is an iterative, compounding process. Each chapter introduces foundational concepts, analyzes architectural trade-offs, and provides concrete technical artifacts that build toward the Capstone Project in Chapter 13.

title: How to Read This Book
text:
Pedagogical Structure
Every chapter in this book follows a consistent, production-tested format:

Foundational Theory: Deep architectural explanation of the subsystem (e.g., how the virtual filesystem layer connects storage drivers to POSIX syscalls).
Comparative Trade-Offs: Real-world case studies comparing how production distributions (Debian, Arch Linux, Alpine Linux, Fedora) solved specific engineering challenges.
Hands-On Recipes: Shell scripts, C snippets, configuration files, and build manifests that you can test and inspect directly.
Troubleshooting & Diagnostics: Practical debugging playbooks explaining common failure modes, diagnostic tools (strace, gdb, dmesg, readelf), and recovery strategies.

title: How to Read This Book
text:
Two Reading Tracks
Depending on your engineering goals, you can navigate this book through two distinct paths:

Track A: The Architectural Explorer
If your primary interest is understanding how Linux works under the hood: - Focus on Chapters 1 through 5 (Kernel, Toolchain, Boot Chain, and Init Systems). - Deep-dive into Chapter 6 (Package Management & SAT Solvers) and Chapter 9 (Security Foundations). - Read the comparative case studies to evaluate why distributions diverged in their architectural choices.


Track B: The Distro Builder
If you intend to produce a functional, bootable distribution: - Read Chapters 1 through 12 sequentially, taking notes on the trade-offs you want for your own system (e.g., glibc vs. musl, systemd vs. OpenRC, binary packages vs. source ports). - Execute Chapter 13 (The Capstone Project) as an end-to-end laboratory, assembling your toolchain, kernel, rootfs, and ISO installer.

title: How to Read This Book
text:
Typographical Conventions
Throughout this book, commands and code blocks follow strict conventions:

Host shell prompts ($): Commands executed on your everyday host workstation:
$ gcc --version
Target chroot / privileged prompts (#): Commands executed within the isolated sysroot or with elevated root privileges:
# chroot /mnt/target /bin/sh
Configuration files: Header comments indicate the exact target filesystem destination:
# /etc/systemd/system/network-setup.service
[Unit]
Description=Minimal Network Setup

Let us begin by dissecting the fundamental anatomy of a Linux operating system.

title: What Makes a Distribution a Distribution
text:
What Makes a Distribution a Distribution
Strictly speaking, Linux is not an operating system. Linux is a monolithic kernel originally written by Linus Torvalds in 1991. The kernel alone cannot provide an interactive user experience, compile code, manage background daemons, or execute commands from a terminal.
A distribution (distro) is an orchestrated collection of software that wraps the Linux kernel into a coherent, functioning operating platform.

title: What Makes a Distribution a Distribution
section: The Defining Pillars of a Distribution
text:
The Defining Pillars of a Distribution
What makes Debian distinct from Arch Linux, or Alpine distinct from Fedora? A distribution’s identity is shaped by six fundamental choices:

1. The C Standard Library (The System ABI)
All userspace software interacts with the Linux kernel through system calls (sys_read, sys_write, sys_clone). The C standard library bridges high-level C code to these low-level assembly traps. - GNU C Library (glibc): Feature-rich, highly optimized for x86_64 and glibc-specific extensions, but large in memory footprint. - musl-libc: Lightweight, clean, POSIX-strict, and designed for static linking and minimal container images (as seen in Alpine Linux).
The choice of C library defines the binary application interface (ABI) of the distribution. A binary compiled dynamically against glibc cannot run on a musl-based system without a compatibility shim.


2. Package Management and Software Delivery
How do users install, upgrade, and delete software? - Debian uses dpkg and apt (.deb). - Red Hat / Fedora uses rpm and dnf (.rpm). - Arch Linux uses pacman (.pkg.tar.zst). - Alpine uses apk-tools (.apk). - Void Linux uses xbps (.xbps).
The package manager dictates how software is packaged, signed, indexed, and resolved against dependencies.


3. The Init System and Service Supervision
Process ID 1 (PID 1) is the first userspace process spawned by the kernel. It has unique kernel responsibilities: - Reaping orphaned child processes. - Managing system state transitions (power-off, reboot, single-user mode). - Launching and supervising background daemons.
Whether a distro uses systemd, OpenRC, s6, runit, or sysvinit drastically changes how daemons are configured, logged, and monitored.


4. Release Philosophy and Lifecycle

Point Releases (Fixed Lifecycle): Debian Stable and Ubuntu LTS release new major versions every two years, prioritizing rock-solid stability and backported security patches over bleeding-edge features.
Rolling Releases: Arch Linux and openSUSE Tumbleweed continuously publish upstream updates without discrete version boundaries.



5. Architectural Boundaries and Policies
Each distribution establishes conventions: Where do configuration files live? Are /bin and /usr/bin separate directories or symlinks? Is SELinux or AppArmor enabled by default? These conventions are codified into the distribution’s policy manuals.

title: The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard and Its Variants
text:
The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard and Its Variants
Every Linux distribution organizes its files within a unified single-rooted hierarchical directory tree (/). The conventions governing where binaries, libraries, configuration files, and state directories reside are defined by the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS), maintained by the Linux Foundation.

title: The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard and Its Variants
text:
The Historical Origin of /bin vs. /usr/bin
Why did Unix-like systems historically have both /bin and /usr/bin, and /lib and /usr/lib?
In the early 1970s, Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie ran out of storage on their PDP-11’s first RK05 disk pack (which held only 1.5 megabytes). They added a second disk pack and mounted it at /usr. Essential commands needed to boot the system into single-user mode and repair filesystems (sh, mount, fsck) stayed in /bin on the primary disk. Everything else (cc, man, troff) moved to /usr.
For decades, this split persisted under the assumption that /usr might be mounted over NFS (Network File System) after the root partition booted.

title: The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard and Its Variants
text:
The Modern “Usr-Merge”
In modern Linux distributions, the /bin vs. /usr/bin distinction is obsolete. Early boot tasks are handled by the initramfs, which mounts all required storage before root pivot occurs.
Consequently, modern distributions (Arch Linux, Fedora, Debian 12+, Ubuntu 20.04+) implement the Usr-Merge:
# On a modern Usr-Merged system:
$ ls -l /
lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root 7 bin -> usr/bin
lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root 7 sbin -> usr/bin
lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root 7 lib -> usr/lib
lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root 9 lib64 -> usr/lib64

Advantages of the Usr-Merge

Simplified $PATH: Developers and scripts no longer have to worry whether a binary is located in /bin, /sbin, /usr/bin, or /usr/sbin.
Snapshotting and Immutable System Roots: The entire operating system binary state is contained within /usr. This allows /usr to be mounted strictly read-only, verified via dm-verity, or updated atomically as an OSTree or Btrfs subvolume.
Clean Factory Resets: Because /usr holds vendor-supplied defaults and /etc holds user overrides, resetting a machine to factory state can be as simple as wiping /etc and /var.

title: Essential Components Every Distro Needs
text:
Essential Components Every Distro Needs
To take an operating system from a blank disk to an interactive command prompt, several independent software projects must be compiled, linked, and arranged into the filesystem tree:

title: Essential Components Every Distro Needs
text:
1. The Core Utility Suite
Users and startup scripts expect standard POSIX utilities (cat, ls, mkdir, rm, chmod, chown). In Linux, these are typically provided by one of two projects:

GNU Coreutils: The standard, fully featured implementations used by Debian, Fedora, and Arch. Includes complete flags, multi-byte character support, and high performance, but binaries are relatively large.
BusyBox / Toybox: Combines tiny versions of hundreds of common UNIX utilities into a single multi-call binary. In BusyBox, /bin/ls is merely a symbolic link to /bin/busybox. Extremely popular in embedded devices, Docker images, and Alpine Linux.

title: Essential Components Every Distro Needs
text:
2. The Dynamic Linker (ld.so)
Most Linux executables are dynamically linked to reduce binary size and allow shared memory caching of library code. When an ELF binary is executed, the kernel reads its .interp section:
$ readelf -l /usr/bin/ls | grep 'program interpreter'
      [Requesting program interpreter: /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2]
The kernel loads this interpreter into memory before executing the binary. If the dynamic linker is missing or placed in an unexpected path, the kernel returns the infamous and misleading error:
bash: ./mybinary: No such file or directory
Even if ./mybinary exists on disk!

title: Essential Components Every Distro Needs
text:
3. Account and Authentication Databases
A minimal system must provide user database files in /etc: - /etc/passwd: Defines user accounts, UIDs, GIDs, home directories, and login shells. - /etc/group: Defines groups and their memberships. - /etc/shadow: Stores hashed passwords and aging parameters (readable only by root). - /etc/nsswitch.conf: Tells the C library which backend databases to query for names (e.g., files, dns, systemd).
A bare-minimum /etc/passwd requires at least:
root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/sh
daemon:x:1:1:daemon:/usr/sbin:/bin/false
nobody:x:65534:65534:nobody:/nonexistent:/bin/false

title: Essential Components Every Distro Needs
text:
4. Virtual Filesystem Mount Points
The Linux kernel exposes device nodes, hardware configurations, and process information via virtual pseudo-filesystems that must be mounted at boot: - /proc: procfs — process state and kernel configuration flags. - /sys: sysfs — unified device model, PCI devices, and driver parameters. - /dev: devtmpfs — automatic device node creation by the kernel. - /dev/pts: devpts — pseudo-terminal slaves for interactive terminal emulators and SSH. - /dev/shm: tmpfs — POSIX shared memory.

title: Case Study: Comparing Debian, Arch, Alpine, and Fedora Layouts
text:
Case Study: Comparing Debian, Arch, Alpine, and Fedora Layouts
To design your own distribution, it is invaluable to examine how leading Linux distributions architected their filesystems, init systems, package managers, and runtime boundaries.

title: Case Study: Comparing Debian, Arch, Alpine, and Fedora Layouts
text:
Debian: Stability and Policy-Driven Engineering
Debian’s layout is governed by the comprehensive Debian Policy Manual. Debian splits upstream software into granular packages (e.g., libssl3 for runtime shared objects, and libssl-dev for headers and static libraries). This keeps production servers minimal by avoiding compiler headers on production nodes. Debian emphasizes backwards compatibility, standard SysV init compatibility shims, and strict multi-architecture support (/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu).

title: Case Study: Comparing Debian, Arch, Alpine, and Fedora Layouts
section: Arch Linux: The Simplicity of “Upstream As-Is”
text:
Arch Linux: The Simplicity of “Upstream As-Is”
Arch follows the KISS principle (Keep It Simple, Stupid). Instead of splitting software into -dev, -doc, and -bin packages, Arch packages upstream software as a single cohesive unit: installing openssl provides the CLI tool, the shared libraries, and the C development headers simultaneously. Arch was one of the earliest adopters of the pure Usr-Merge, collapsing all binaries into /usr/bin.

title: Case Study: Comparing Debian, Arch, Alpine, and Fedora Layouts
section: Alpine Linux: Extreme Minimalism with musl
text:
Alpine Linux: Extreme Minimalism with musl
Alpine targets containers, embedded systems, and security enclaves. By replacing glibc with musl and GNU coreutils with BusyBox, a basic Alpine rootfs occupies under 7 megabytes of uncompressed disk space. Alpine avoids systemd in favor of OpenRC, keeping startup scripts transparent and POSIX shell-driven. However, dynamic linking against musl requires software compiled specifically for the musl ABI.

title: Case Study: Comparing Debian, Arch, Alpine, and Fedora Layouts
section: Fedora: Upstream Pioneer and Modern Security
text:
Fedora: Upstream Pioneer and Modern Security
Fedora serves as the upstream proving ground for Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL). It is aggressively modern: Wayland is default, legacy X11 packages are phased out, Btrfs with transparent zstd compression is the default filesystem, and SELinux is set to Enforcing out of the box. Fedora also pioneered systemd-resolved and systemd-homed integrations.

title: Case Study: Comparing Debian, Arch, Alpine, and Fedora Layouts
text:
Lessons for Your Distribution
When designing your own distribution in Chapter 13: 1. Choose your C library based on your mission: Choose musl if you want a tiny footprint, instant boot times, or an embedded appliance. Choose glibc if you need broad proprietary software compatibility (NVIDIA drivers, Steam, precompiled enterprise software). 2. Embrace the Usr-Merge: Symlinking /bin, /sbin, and /lib into /usr radically simplifies package creation, script path lookups, and system snapshotting.

title: Monolithic Architecture with Modular Extensions
text:
Monolithic Architecture with Modular Extensions
Operating system kernels generally fall into two classic design philosophies: microkernels and monolithic kernels.

title: Monolithic Architecture with Modular Extensions
text:
Why Linux is Monolithic
In a pure microkernel, device drivers, filesystems, and network stacks run as isolated userspace server processes. While this isolates faults (a driver crash won’t crash the entire kernel), passing data across user-kernel boundaries requires expensive context switches and inter-process communication (IPC) overhead.
Linux is a monolithic kernel: - All core operating system services—process scheduling, memory allocation, virtual filesystems, network protocols, and hardware device drivers—execute within a single unified address space in supervisor mode (Ring 0 on x86). - System calls (syscall) transition the CPU from user mode (Ring 3) directly into kernel mode with minimal overhead. - Direct pointer dereferencing within kernel space makes Linux extraordinarily fast and responsive.

title: Monolithic Architecture with Modular Extensions
text:
Loadable Kernel Modules (LKMs)
A purely static monolithic kernel would require recompiling and rebooting the entire operating system every time a new USB device, network card, or filesystem was attached.
To achieve flexibility without sacrificing bare-metal speed, Linux introduced Loadable Kernel Modules (LKMs): - Code compiled into .ko (Kernel Object) ELF binaries. - Dynamically inserted into the running kernel using init_module or finit_module syscalls (insmod or modprobe). - Linked into kernel memory at runtime, running with full Ring 0 privileges.
# Listing currently loaded modules in the running kernel:
$ lsmod | head -n 5
Module                  Size  Used by
overlay               151552  0
ext4                 1052672  1
crc32c_generic         16384  0
ahci                   45056  2

title: Monolithic Architecture with Modular Extensions
text:
Built-In (=y) vs. Modular (=m) Drivers
When configuring a custom kernel for your distribution, you will constantly choose between: - =y (Built-in): The code is compiled directly into the executable kernel image (vmlinuz). It is permanently resident in RAM from boot time. - =m (Module): The code is compiled into a standalone /lib/modules/<version>/.../*.ko file on disk. It is loaded on demand when the hardware is discovered by udev.

The Golden Rule for Distribution Builders
If a driver is strictly necessary to mount the root filesystem (e.g., your SATA/NVMe controller driver, your root filesystem driver like ext4 or btrfs), it must either be compiled as built-in (=y) or included inside the initramfs. If it is compiled as =m and left on the root disk, the kernel cannot read the disk to load the driver needed to read the disk!

title: Key Subsystems: Process Management, Memory, VFS, Networking
text:
Key Subsystems: Process Management, Memory, VFS, Networking
The Linux kernel is comprised of millions of lines of C and assembly code, cleanly organized into several primary subsystems.

title: Key Subsystems: Process Management, Memory, VFS, Networking
text:
1. Process Management & Scheduling
Every thread in Linux is represented by a kernel structure called struct task_struct (defined in <linux/sched.h>). It contains process state, priority, open file descriptors, signal masks, memory descriptors (mm_struct), and namespace mappings.

The Scheduler (EEVDF): Starting with Linux 6.6, the kernel default scheduler is the Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First (EEVDF) scheduler, replacing the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS). EEVDF allocates CPU time slices based on virtual runtime and eligibility deadlines, guaranteeing low latency for interactive audio and desktop tasks while maintaining fair throughput for batch computation.
Control Groups (cgroups v2): Hierarchically accounts for and throttles resource consumption (CPU shares, memory caps, I/O limits, PID limits) for groups of processes. Crucial for systemd service isolation and container runtimes.

title: Key Subsystems: Process Management, Memory, VFS, Networking
text:
2. Memory Management (MM)
Linux implements a virtual memory system with demand paging: - Virtual Address Spaces: Every 64-bit userspace process enjoys a private virtual address space (typically 128 TB on x86_64 48-bit paging). - Page Tables: Hardware MMU (Memory Management Unit) translates virtual addresses to physical RAM pages (usually 4 KB, or HugePages of 2 MB / 1 GB). - The Page Cache: The kernel uses all unused physical RAM as a buffer cache for disk reads and writes. Dirty pages are written back to storage asynchronously by kernel flush threads. - The OOM Killer (Out-of-Memory): If system memory and swap are exhausted, the kernel’s Out-Of-Memory Killer evaluates process badness scores and sends SIGKILL to reclaim memory.

title: Key Subsystems: Process Management, Memory, VFS, Networking
text:
3. The Virtual Filesystem (VFS)
The Virtual Filesystem (VFS) provides a standardized object-oriented abstraction over heterogeneous storage formats (ext4, XFS, Btrfs, NFS, FAT32): - Superblock: Describes an entire mounted filesystem instance. - Inode: Represents a unique file or directory object on disk, storing metadata (size, permissions, timestamps, block pointers) independent of the file’s name. - Dentry (Directory Entry): Caches the mapping between human-readable path strings (/usr/bin/python3) and underlying inode numbers in memory. - File: Represents an active file descriptor held by an open process, tracking the current byte read/write offset.

title: Key Subsystems: Process Management, Memory, VFS, Networking
text:
4. The Network Stack
The Linux networking stack processes packets through an event-driven subsystem: - Socket Interface: POSIX API (socket(), bind(), listen(), accept(), send(), recv()). - Protocol Engines: TCP, UDP, ICMP, SCTP, and raw sockets. - Netfilter / nftables: In-kernel packet filtering, stateful connection tracking (conntrack), and NAT (Network Address Translation). - eBPF (Extended Berkeley Packet Filter): In-kernel virtual machine executing sandboxed bytecode at line rate on network hooks (XDP - eXpress Data Path).

title: Kernel Configuration and the .config Workflow
text:
Kernel Configuration and the .config Workflow
The Linux kernel contains over 15,000 configurable options defined in a domain-specific language called Kconfig. The entire state of a build is recorded in a single plaintext file at the root of the kernel tree named .config.

title: Kernel Configuration and the .config Workflow
text:
Navigating the Configuration Interfaces
The kernel build system (Kbuild) provides several interfaces for configuring features:
# Interactive curses-based menu (most popular for distro builders):
$ make menuconfig

# Qt-based graphical interface:
$ make xconfig

# Generate a default configuration based on your CPU architecture:
$ make defconfig

# Generate a minimal configuration matching currently loaded modules on host:
$ make localmodconfig

# Update an older .config against a newly extracted kernel version:
$ make olddefconfig

title: Kernel Configuration and the .config Workflow
text:
Anatomy of .config
Inside .config, options follow a simple key-value format:
# A boolean option enabled statically in kernel:
CONFIG_BINFMT_ELF=y

# A tri-state option built as a loadable module:
CONFIG_EXT4_FS=m

# A disabled option (not compiled):
# CONFIG_EXT2_FS is not set

# An integer configuration parameter:
CONFIG_NR_CPUS=64

# A string parameter (e.g., custom distro kernel release tag):
CONFIG_LOCALVERSION="-byol-v1"

title: Kernel Configuration and the .config Workflow
section: Mandatory Options for a Bootable Modern Distro
text:
Mandatory Options for a Bootable Modern Distro
When building a distribution kernel from scratch, disabling certain options will cause immediate boot failures:

Executable Formats:

CONFIG_BINFMT_ELF=y: Essential for running standard Linux binaries.
CONFIG_BINFMT_SCRIPT=y: Essential for interpreting #!/bin/sh scripts.

Virtual Filesystems:

CONFIG_DEVTMPFS=y and CONFIG_DEVTMPFS_MOUNT=y: Tells the kernel to mount /dev automatically at boot.
CONFIG_PROC_FS=y and CONFIG_SYSFS=y.

Storage & Controller Drivers:

CONFIG_BLK_DEV_SD=y: SCSI/SATA disk support.
CONFIG_ATA=y and CONFIG_ATA_GENERIC=y.
CONFIG_NVME_CORE=y: Modern NVMe SSD support.
CONFIG_VIRTIO_PCI=y and CONFIG_VIRTIO_BLK=y: Essential for QEMU/KVM virtual machine testing.

Filesystem Drivers:

CONFIG_EXT4_FS=y or CONFIG_BTRFS_FS=y: Compiled as =y (built-in) if booting without an initramfs, or =m if the initramfs contains the driver.

title: Kernel Configuration and the .config Workflow
text:
Compiling the Kernel Image
Once .config is validated:
# Build the compressed kernel image and modules (-j$(nproc) uses all CPU cores):
$ make -j$(nproc) bzImage
$ make -j$(nproc) modules

# Install kernel modules into the target sysroot:
$ make INSTALL_MOD_PATH=/mnt/target modules_install

# Copy the kernel image into the boot directory:
$ cp arch/x86/boot/bzImage /mnt/target/boot/vmlinuz-byol

title: Troubleshooting: Diagnosing Kernel Panics
text:
Troubleshooting: Diagnosing Kernel Panics
A kernel panic occurs when the Linux kernel encounters an unrecoverable internal condition or fatal hardware error from which it cannot safely recover. Unlike a userspace segmentation fault (which simply terminates the offending process), a kernel panic halts the entire operating system to prevent disk corruption.

title: Troubleshooting: Diagnosing Kernel Panics
text:
Anatomy of the Panic Message
When a panic occurs, the kernel dumps diagnostic state directly to the console framebuffer or serial port:
[    1.120340] Call Trace:
[    1.121002]  <TASK>
[    1.121500]  dump_stack_lvl+0x44/0x60
[    1.122100]  panic+0x140/0x320
[    1.122700]  mount_block_root+0x1a8/0x220
[    1.123300]  mount_root+0x9c/0x130
[    1.123900]  prepare_namespace+0x13c/0x170
[    1.124500]  kernel_init+0x18/0x140
[    1.125100]  ret_from_fork+0x28/0x40
[    1.125700]  </TASK>
The stack trace reveals the exact sequence of functions leading up to the failure. In the example above, prepare_namespace called mount_root, which failed and triggered panic().

title: Troubleshooting: Diagnosing Kernel Panics
section: Common Panic Scenarios for Distro Builders
text:
Common Panic Scenarios for Distro Builders

1. VFS: Unable to mount root fs on unknown-block(0,0)
This is by far the most common panic encountered by operating system builders. It means the kernel was instructed to mount a root partition (root=/dev/sda1 or root=UUID=...), but could not locate or open the device.
Root Causes & Solutions: - Missing disk controller driver: The SATA (ahci), NVMe (nvme), or Virtual VirtIO (virtio_pci, virtio_blk) driver was compiled as a module (=m) instead of built-in (=y), and no initramfs was loaded. Fix: Recompile driver with =y or pack it into the initramfs. - Missing filesystem driver: The root filesystem is formatted as ext4, but CONFIG_EXT4_FS is =m or not set. Fix: Set CONFIG_EXT4_FS=y. - Incorrect root= kernel parameter: The UUID or device node specified in the bootloader does not match the actual disk geometry.


2. Kernel panic - not syncing: Attempted to kill init!
The kernel successfully mounted the root filesystem, found the binary at /sbin/init (or /bin/sh), and executed it. However, PID 1 died or returned. PID 1 is never allowed to exit in Linux. If PID 1 terminates, the kernel panics immediately.
Root Causes & Solutions: - Missing dynamic linker: The init binary was dynamically linked against /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2, but the linker does not exist at that path in the target rootfs. - Missing shared libraries: The init binary links against libc.so.6, but it is missing from /lib or /usr/lib. - Wrong CPU architecture: Running an x86_64 binary on a 32-bit kernel, or an aarch64 binary without an emulator. - Execution permissions: The init binary lacks execute permissions (chmod +x /sbin/init).

title: Troubleshooting: Diagnosing Kernel Panics
text:
Diagnostic Tools

Early Printk: Add earlyprintk=vga or earlycon and console=ttyS0,115200 to the kernel command line in your bootloader. This prints kernel messages even if the graphics framebuffer crashes early.
QEMU Serial Redirection: When testing your kernel in QEMU, redirect serial output to the terminal:
$ qemu-system-x86_64 -kernel bzImage -append "console=ttyS0 root=/dev/vda" -nographic
Panic Timeout: Add panic=10 to reboot automatically 10 seconds after a panic, or panic=-1 to freeze the screen for manual inspection.

title: What a Toolchain Is and Why It Matters
text:
What a Toolchain Is and Why It Matters
A toolchain is the collection of software development utilities that transforms human-readable source code into executable binary machine instructions for a target architecture.

title: What a Toolchain Is and Why It Matters
section: Anatomy of a GNU / Linux Toolchain
text:
Anatomy of a GNU / Linux Toolchain
A standard Linux toolchain consists of four interdependent components:

Linux Kernel Headers (linux-api-headers): Cleaned C header files from the kernel source tree (<linux/types.h>, <asm/unistd.h>). These headers define the system call numbers, ioctl codes, and kernel structures required by the C standard library.
GNU Binutils: The binary manipulation suite, including:

as: The assembler that turns assembly code into machine object files (.o).
ld: The linker that joins object files and shared libraries into an ELF executable.
readelf, objdump, nm, strip, ar, ranlib.

GCC (GNU Compiler Collection): The optimizing compiler that translates C/C++ syntax into architecture-specific assembly instructions.
The C Standard Library (glibc or musl): Provides the standard C runtime (printf, malloc, fopen), dynamic startup code (crt1.o, crti.o, crtn.o), and the dynamic linker/loader (ld-linux.so).

title: What a Toolchain Is and Why It Matters
text:
Host, Build, and Target Triples
In GNU autotools, cross-compilation is governed by standard architecture-vendor-os tuples known as target triples:

Build (--build): The architecture and OS of the machine where the compilation is currently running (e.g., x86_64-pc-linux-gnu).
Host (--host): The architecture and OS of the machine where the compiled binary will execute.
Target (--target): The architecture and OS for which the compiler will generate machine code. (Only relevant when building a compiler like GCC).

Host == Build == Target  --> Native Compiler (Standard host GCC)
Host == Build != Target  --> Cross-Compiler (Runs on host, compiles for target)
Host != Build == Target  --> Canadian Cross (Runs on host B, built on host A, targets host B)
In Chapter 13, we construct a cross-compiler with: - --host=x86_64-pc-linux-gnu - --target=x86_64-byol-linux-gnu (or x86_64-byol-linux-musl) This ensures the compiler does not accidentally link against the host system’s headers or libraries.

title: The Bootstrap Process: Pass One and Pass Two
text:
The Bootstrap Process: Pass One and Pass Two
Bootstrapping a new distribution presents a circular dependency problem: - To build the C library (glibc), you need a C compiler (gcc). - To build a functional C compiler (gcc), you need the C library headers and startup objects (libc.so, crt1.o).
To break this loop without poisoning the target distribution with host binaries, distro builders employ a multi-pass bootstrap process.

title: The Bootstrap Process: Pass One and Pass Two
text:
Pass 1: The Bare-Metal Cross-Compiler
In Pass 1, we compile a stripped-down, static cross-compiler that runs on the host system:

Install Linux API Headers: Extract kernel headers directly into $SYSROOT/usr/include.
$ make mrproper
$ make headers_install INSTALL_HDR_PATH=$SYSROOT/usr
Build Cross-Binutils (Pass 1): Configured with --target=$TARGET and --with-sysroot=$SYSROOT.
$ ../binutils/configure \
    --prefix=$TOOLS \
    --with-sysroot=$SYSROOT \
    --target=$TARGET \
    --disable-nls \
    --disable-werror
$ make && make install
Build GCC (Pass 1 - Static / Inhibit libc): Configure GCC with --without-headers, --with-newlib, and --disable-shared. This builds a bare C-only compiler without thread support or dynamic linking capabilities:
$ ../gcc/configure \
    --target=$TARGET \
    --prefix=$TOOLS \
    --with-glibc-version=2.39 \
    --with-sysroot=$SYSROOT \
    --without-headers \
    --disable-nls \
    --disable-shared \
    --disable-threads \
    --enable-languages=c
$ make all-gcc all-target-libgcc && make install-gcc install-target-libgcc

title: The Bootstrap Process: Pass One and Pass Two
section: The Intermediate Bridge: Compiling the Target C Library
text:
The Intermediate Bridge: Compiling the Target C Library
Now that we possess $TOOLS/bin/$TARGET-gcc (a compiler capable of emitting target machine code without needing a pre-existing target libc), we compile glibc or musl:
$ CC="$TARGET-gcc" ../glibc/configure \
    --prefix=/usr \
    --host=$TARGET \
    --build=$(../glibc/scripts/config.guess) \
    --enable-kernel=4.19 \
    --with-headers=$SYSROOT/usr/include \
    libc_cv_slibdir=/usr/lib
$ make && make DESTDIR=$SYSROOT install

title: The Bootstrap Process: Pass One and Pass Two
section: Pass 2: The Full Cross-Compiler and Native Chroot Tools
text:
Pass 2: The Full Cross-Compiler and Native Chroot Tools
With the target C library now safely installed inside $SYSROOT/usr/lib and $SYSROOT/usr/include:

Rebuild GCC (Pass 2): Build a full compiler targeting $TARGET with C++ support, thread support (pthreads), and shared library support enabled.
Compile Core Utilities for Target: Using the Pass 2 cross-compiler, build Bash, Coreutils, Sed, Grep, Gawk, and Make, installing them into $SYSROOT.
The Pivot (Entering Chroot): Mount host /dev, /proc, and /sys into $SYSROOT and switch into the target rootfs using chroot:
# chroot $SYSROOT /usr/bin/bash
From this point forward, every package is compiled natively from inside the clean environment. The host system’s tools are severed.

title: glibc vs. musl: Choosing Your C Standard Library
text:
glibc vs. musl: Choosing Your C Standard Library
The C standard library is the foundation of the Linux userspace ABI. In modern distribution engineering, the two leading implementations are the GNU C Library (glibc) and musl-libc.

title: glibc vs. musl: Choosing Your C Standard Library
text:
The GNU C Library (glibc)
glibc is the default standard library on virtually all desktop and enterprise Linux distributions.

Strengths:

Peak Execution Performance: Highly hand-tuned assembly implementations for SIMD string operations (avx2, avx512 accelerated memcpy, strlen, strcmp).
Maximum Compatibility: Seamlessly runs proprietary closed-source applications (Oracle Database, Steam games, NVIDIA CUDA toolkits, Electron apps) which rely on GNU-specific symbol versioning.
NSS (Name Service Switch): Dynamic module-based identity and name resolution via /etc/nsswitch.conf (libnss_files.so, libnss_dns.so, libnss_systemd.so).



Weaknesses:

Static linking is notoriously fragile: because NSS plugins rely on dlopen(), statically linked glibc binaries still require dynamic linker access at runtime to resolve hostnames.
Large binary size and memory footprint.

title: glibc vs. musl: Choosing Your C Standard Library
text:
musl-libc
Written by Rich Felker, musl is a clean, lightweight, standards-conforming implementation of the C library designed for correctness, safety, and minimalism.

Strengths:

Flawless Static Linking: A statically linked C executable under musl is truly standalone. It contains zero external dynamic dependencies and will run on any Linux kernel without an installed libc.
Microscopic Footprint: Ideal for container base images, micro-VMs (Firecracker), and embedded microcontrollers.
Hardened Memory Safety: musl’s mallocng allocator is engineered with guard pages and randomized layout to detect heap overflows and double-frees reliably.



Weaknesses:

Software with hardcoded __GLIBC__ macros or non-POSIX assumptions (e.g., expecting execinfo.h for backtraces) will fail to compile without patches.
DNS resolution does not support NSS plugins; it queries /etc/resolv.conf directly.

title: glibc vs. musl: Choosing Your C Standard Library
text:
Verdict for BYOL Builders

If your goal is a general-purpose workstation or server compatible with off-the-shelf software and precompiled binaries: choose glibc.
If your goal is an immutable appliance, container base, or ultra-lightweight router: choose musl.

title: Case Study: Alpine’s musl-Based Hardened Toolchain
text:
Case Study: Alpine’s musl-Based Hardened Toolchain
Alpine Linux is widely celebrated in modern cloud infrastructure as the de facto lightweight container base image. However, Alpine’s primary engineering objective was not small size; it was security hardening.

title: Case Study: Alpine’s musl-Based Hardened Toolchain
text:
The Alpine Toolchain Architecture
Alpine maintains its own patched build of GCC configured with aggressive compile-time and link-time flags enabled by default:

Default PIE (Position Independent Executable):

By default, standard GCC compiles binaries to execute at fixed virtual memory addresses.
Alpine GCC compiles every single userland binary as a shared object (-fPIE -pie). This allows the kernel’s Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) to randomize the memory address of the executable text, stack, and heap on every invocation, neutralizing Return-Oriented Programming (ROP) exploits.

Stack Smashing Protection (SSP):

Alpine enables -fstack-protector-strong by default.
The compiler injects canary values onto the stack frame between local buffers and the saved return pointer. If a buffer overflow overwrites the return pointer, the canary is mangled, triggering __stack_chk_fail and aborting the process before malicious code executes.

Full RELRO (Read-Only Relocations) & BIND_NOW:

In standard binaries (Partial RELRO), the Global Offset Table (GOT) remains writable during execution to allow lazy symbol binding by ld.so.
Alpine enforces -Wl,-z,relro -Wl,-z,now. All dynamic symbols are resolved immediately at launch time, and the entire GOT page is marked read-only before main() begins. This eliminates GOT-overwrite attacks.

title: Case Study: Alpine’s musl-Based Hardened Toolchain
text:
The Cost of Hardening
Compiling an entire operating system with strict POSIX compliance and defensive security boundaries reveals software defects: - Upstream projects frequently rely on undefined behavior or GNU extensions without realizing it. - When Alpine builds software via abuild, its maintainers maintain a collection of surgical C patches to resolve these assumptions cleanly.
In Chapter 9 and Chapter 13, we adopt several of these hardening flags for our BYOL toolchain.

title: Troubleshooting: Toolchain Build Failures
text:
Troubleshooting: Toolchain Build Failures
Building a compiler and C standard library from scratch pushes build environments to their limits. A single missing dependency, poisoned environment variable, or hardcoded path can corrupt hours of compilation.

title: Troubleshooting: Toolchain Build Failures
text:
Common Toolchain Failure Modes

1. Host Pollution (The Inadvertent Leak)
Symptom: A binary compiled in your isolated target sysroot unexpectedly depends on a host library or dynamic linker:
$ readelf -d /mnt/target/bin/bash | grep NEEDED
 0x0000000000000001 (NEEDED)             Shared library: [libtinfo.so.6]
$ readelf -l /mnt/target/bin/bash | grep interpreter
      [Requesting program interpreter: /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2] # (Points to host!)
Cause: The compiler invoked during the build process was /usr/bin/gcc (the host compiler) instead of $TARGET-gcc, or the linker used /usr/lib from the host search path. Remedy: - Always sanitize your shell environment before toolchain builds: bash   unset CFLAGS CXXFLAGS LDFLAGS   export LC_ALL=POSIX   export PATH=$TOOLS/bin:/usr/bin:/bin - Use readelf -l <binary> to inspect the ELF program interpreter of every compiled utility before moving forward.


2. Missing C Preprocessor Prerequisites for GCC
Symptom: GCC configuration fails with:
configure: error: Building GCC requires GMP 4.2+, MPFR 3.1.0+ and MPC 0.8.0+.
Cause: GCC’s internal optimization passes rely on multi-precision arithmetic libraries (GMP, MPFR, MPC). Remedy: Rather than installing them on the host, place their source directories directly inside the GCC source root:
$ tar -xf mpfr-4.2.1.tar.xz && mv mpfr-4.2.1 gcc-14.1.0/mpfr
$ tar -xf gmp-6.3.0.tar.xz && mv gmp-6.3.0 gcc-14.1.0/gmp
$ tar -xf mpc-1.3.1.tar.gz && mv mpc-1.3.1 gcc-14.1.0/mpc
GCC’s build system will automatically compile these libraries statically within its own build tree.


3. Missing crt1.o or Linker Script Failures
Symptom: During Pass 2, compilation fails with:
/tools/lib/gcc/x86_64-byol-linux-gnu/14.1.0/../../../../x86_64-byol-linux-gnu/bin/ld: cannot find crt1.o: No such file or directory
Cause: The C runtime startup files (crt1.o, crti.o, crtn.o) were installed into /usr/lib, but the cross-linker is searching /lib or has a mismatched --sysroot prefix. Remedy: Verify your $SYSROOT/usr/lib directory contains the startup object files, and verify that your specs file or linker invocation points to the appropriate sysroot:
$ $TARGET-gcc -print-file-name=crt1.o
If this prints the correct path inside $SYSROOT, the compiler knows where its runtime objects reside.

title: From Power-On to Shell: The Full Boot Chain
text:
From Power-On to Shell: The Full Boot Chain
The journey from pressing the physical power button on a computer to receiving an interactive shell prompt involves a relay race of hardware, firmware, bootloaders, kernel subsystems, and userspace processes.

title: From Power-On to Shell: The Full Boot Chain
text:
The Baton Pass
Notice how every stage has a single purpose: load the next, more capable stage, and get out of the way: 1. UEFI initializes basic memory and PCI buses, then launches the bootloader. 2. The bootloader reads the filesystem of /boot, loads the compressed kernel and initramfs into memory, and jumps to the kernel’s entry point. 3. The kernel initializes drivers and memory, then executes /init inside the temporary in-memory initramfs. 4. The initramfs script resolves complex storage (decryption, RAID assembly, network mounts), mounts the permanent root disk, and executes switch_root. 5. switch_root wipes the temporary initramfs from memory and replaces the running process with the real /sbin/init (PID 1). 6. PID 1 manages services, configures networking, and spawns login prompts.

title: BIOS, UEFI, and the EFI System Partition
text:
BIOS, UEFI, and the EFI System Partition
Before operating systems run, firmware governs the machine. Understanding firmware architecture is essential when designing bootable installation media.

title: BIOS, UEFI, and the EFI System Partition
text:
Legacy BIOS (Basic Input/Output System)
For over thirty years, IBM PC-compatible machines booted via Legacy BIOS: - 16-bit Real Mode: The CPU started in 16-bit real mode with access to only 1 MB of RAM. - Master Boot Record (MBR): The BIOS read the first 512-byte sector of the boot drive into memory address 0x7C00. - Constraint: The MBR contained partition table definitions and machine code. Because 512 bytes is too small for a modern filesystem driver, bootloaders required multi-stage hacks (Stage 1 in MBR sector 0, Stage 1.5 in post-MBR gap, Stage 2 in /boot). - Disk Limit: MBR partition tables cannot address disks larger than 2.2 Terabytes (32-bit sector addressing).

title: BIOS, UEFI, and the EFI System Partition
text:
Modern UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface)
Modern systems boot using UEFI: - Native 64-bit Architecture: Runs in 64-bit protected mode from the first instruction with full access to system RAM. - GPT (GUID Partition Table): Supports disks up to 9.4 Zettabytes and up to 128 primary partitions with unique 128-bit GUIDs. - Built-in Filesystem Driver: UEFI firmware natively understands the FAT32 filesystem!

title: BIOS, UEFI, and the EFI System Partition
text:
The EFI System Partition (ESP)
Under UEFI, the firmware does not execute raw binary sectors from disk blocks. Instead, it inspects GPT partition headers to find a partition with the specific GUID C12A7328-F81F-11D2-BA4B-00A0C93EC93B (the EFI System Partition, or ESP), formatted as FAT32 (or FAT16).
ESP Partition (Mounted at /boot/efi or /boot)
└── EFI/
    ├── BOOT/
    │   └── BOOTX64.EFI        # Default fallback EFI binary
    ├── byol/
    │   └── grubx64.efi        # Custom distro bootloader
    └── Linux/
        └── vmlinuz.efi        # EFISTUB direct kernel binary

The Default Fallback Path
When a removable USB stick or DVD is inserted, the firmware does not know which OS is installed. The UEFI specification mandates a standard fallback path for x86_64 machines:
/EFI/BOOT/BOOTX64.EFI
On aarch64 (ARM64), this file is /EFI/BOOT/BOOTAA64.EFI. When authoring an ISO or USB installer in Chapter 10, placing your bootloader at this exact path ensures it boots seamlessly on any UEFI hardware.

title: BIOS, UEFI, and the EFI System Partition
text:
NVRAM Boot Entries and efibootmgr
UEFI motherboards maintain non-volatile RAM (NVRAM) storing boot priority entries. You can inspect and modify these from Linux using efibootmgr:
# Listing boot entries:
$ efibootmgr -v
BootCurrent: 0001
BootOrder: 0001,0002,0000
Boot0001* BYOL Linux   HD(1,GPT,a48f...)/File(\EFI\byol\grubx64.efi)

# Creating a new boot entry for BYOL:
$ efibootmgr --create --disk /dev/nvme0n1 --part 1 \
    --label "BYOL Linux" \
    --loader '\EFI\byol\grubx64.efi'

title: GRUB, systemd-boot, and Other Bootloaders
text:
GRUB, systemd-boot, and Other Bootloaders
The bootloader bridges firmware and the Linux kernel. When engineering a distribution, you must choose a bootloader that matches your system architecture and hardware compatibility requirements.

title: GRUB, systemd-boot, and Other Bootloaders
text:
GRUB 2 (Grand Unified Bootloader)
GRUB 2 is the most powerful and versatile bootloader in the Linux ecosystem.

Key Capabilities:

Operates as a mini-operating system with its own memory management, terminal emulator, graphics engine, and dynamic modules (.mod).
Understands complex filesystems directly. GRUB can load a kernel located inside a software RAID (mdadm), LVM volume group, encrypted LUKS container, or Btrfs subvolume.
Supports both legacy BIOS (i386-pc) and 32/64-bit UEFI (x86_64-efi, i386-efi, arm64-efi).



GRUB Configuration (grub.cfg)
# /boot/grub/grub.cfg
set timeout=5
set default=0

menuentry "BYOL Linux (Rolling)" {
    insmod gzio
    insmod part_gpt
    insmod ext2
    search --no-floppy --fs-uuid --set=root a4b2-8c11-deadbeef
    linux /boot/vmlinuz-byol root=UUID=a4b2-8c11-deadbeef rw quiet console=tty0
    initrd /boot/initramfs-byol.img
}

title: GRUB, systemd-boot, and Other Bootloaders
text:
systemd-boot (Formerly Gummiboot)
If your distribution targets modern UEFI systems exclusively, systemd-boot offers clean, minimalist elegance: - It relies entirely on the UEFI firmware’s built-in FAT32 filesystem driver. - It contains no filesystem drivers or scripting engines. It simply presents a menu of boot entries and invokes the kernel using the UEFI EFISTUB protocol.

Boot Loader Specification (BLS)
systemd-boot complies with the standard Boot Loader Specification. Adding a new kernel requires dropping a small .conf file into /boot/loader/entries/:
# /boot/loader/entries/byol-6.10.conf
title   BYOL Linux
version 6.10.2
linux   /vmlinuz-6.10.2
initrd  /initramfs-6.10.2.img
options root=UUID=23b49e8a-1209 rw quiet

title: GRUB, systemd-boot, and Other Bootloaders
text:
Other Notable Bootloaders

Syslinux / Isolinux: Extremely popular for generating bootable live CDs and hybrid ISO images due to its tiny footprint and robust El Torito emulation.
Limine: A modern, high-performance, open-source bootloader supporting BIOS, UEFI, and advanced protocols.
U-Boot (Universal Boot Loader): The undisputed standard bootloader for embedded ARM boards, Raspberry Pi, and RISC-V development platforms.

title: Creating a Custom Initramfs
text:
Creating a Custom Initramfs
The initramfs (Initial RAM Filesystem) is a compressed CPIO archive containing a complete, tiny userspace environment that the bootloader loads into physical RAM alongside the kernel image.

title: Creating a Custom Initramfs
text:
Why an Initramfs is Necessary
In a simple development setup, the kernel could mount /dev/sda1 directly if its driver was compiled statically (=y). But in real-world systems, mounting the root filesystem requires complex userspace logic: - The disk might be an encrypted LUKS volume requiring a password prompt or TPM2 key unsealing. - The root might be an LVM logical volume or mdadm software RAID requiring scanning and activation. - The root might be on an NFS share or iSCSI SAN requiring DHCP lease acquisition. - Hardware device nodes are dynamic and require udev or mdev to settle.
The kernel delegates all this complexity to an early userspace script: /init.

title: Creating a Custom Initramfs
section: Building a Minimal Initramfs by Hand
text:
Building a Minimal Initramfs by Hand
To truly understand how early boot works, we will construct a custom initramfs using BusyBox:

Step 1: Create the Directory Tree
$ mkdir -p initramfs-root/{bin,sbin,etc,proc,sys,dev,newroot}


Step 2: Install BusyBox
Copy a statically linked busybox binary and create symlinks:
$ cp /bin/busybox initramfs-root/bin/
$ cd initramfs-root/bin
$ ln -s busybox sh
$ ln -s busybox mount
$ ln -s busybox umount
$ ln -s busybox switch_root
$ ln -s busybox sleep
$ cd ../..


Step 3: Write the /init Script
Create an executable script at initramfs-root/init:
#!/bin/sh
# /init — BYOL Early Userspace Boot Script
echo "========================================="
echo "   Welcome to BYOL Linux (Early Boot)    "
echo "========================================="

# 1. Mount virtual kernel filesystems
mount -t proc none /proc
mount -t sysfs none /sys
mount -t devtmpfs none /dev

# 2. Parse kernel command line for root= parameter
ROOT_DEV=""
for param in $(cat /proc/cmdline); do
    case "$param" in
        root=*) ROOT_DEV="${param#root=}" ;;
    esac
done

echo "[initramfs] Mounting real root: $ROOT_DEV to /newroot..."
# Wait for storage devices to settle
sleep 1

# 3. Mount real root disk
mount -o ro "$ROOT_DEV" /newroot
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
    echo "[initramfs] FATAL: Failed to mount root filesystem!"
    echo "[initramfs] Dropping into rescue emergency shell..."
    exec /bin/sh
fi

# 4. Clean up mounts before switch_root
umount /proc
umount /sys
umount /dev

# 5. Pivot into permanent rootfs and invoke real PID 1
echo "[initramfs] Handing execution over to /sbin/init..."
exec switch_root /newroot /sbin/init
Ensure the script has executable permissions:
$ chmod +x initramfs-root/init


Step 4: Pack into a Compressed CPIO Archive
The kernel expects the archive in standard newc CPIO format:
$ cd initramfs-root
$ find . -print0 | cpio --null --create --format=newc | gzip -9 > ../initramfs.img
In under 2 megabytes, you have engineered a fully functional early boot environment!

title: Troubleshooting: Boot Chain Failures
text:
Troubleshooting: Boot Chain Failures
Diagnosing boot failures requires isolating which phase of the boot chain experienced the breakdown:

title: Troubleshooting: Boot Chain Failures
text:
Phase 1: Firmware / Bootloader Errors

“No bootable device found” or dropping into UEFI Shell

Root Cause: The ESP partition does not exist, is formatted as NTFS/ext4 instead of FAT32, or the file /EFI/BOOT/BOOTX64.EFI is missing.
Diagnostic: In the UEFI shell, type fs0: followed by ls EFI\BOOT to confirm the presence of the EFI binary.



grub rescue> error: unknown filesystem

Root Cause: GRUB’s Stage 1 booted from the MBR/ESP, but it cannot read the partition containing /boot/grub because the filesystem module (ext2.mod, btrfs.mod) is not accessible.
Remedy from Rescue Shell:
grub rescue> ls
(hd0) (hd0,gpt1) (hd0,gpt2)
grub rescue> ls (hd0,gpt2)/
grub rescue> set root=(hd0,gpt2)
grub rescue> set prefix=(hd0,gpt2)/boot/grub
grub rescue> insmod normal
grub rescue> normal

title: Troubleshooting: Boot Chain Failures
text:
Phase 2: Initramfs & Switch Root Failures

Dropping into the Emergency Rescue Shell
If your /init script contains exec /bin/sh on error, you will see a rescue prompt:
[initramfs] FATAL: Failed to mount root filesystem!
/bin/sh: can't access tty; job control turned off
#
Diagnostic Steps: 1. Check available block devices: sh    # cat /proc/partitions    # ls -l /dev/sd* /dev/nvme* /dev/vd* 2. Manually test mounting: sh    # mount /dev/vda2 /newroot 3. If /dev/vda2 does not exist: the storage driver module was not loaded. Verify whether modprobe virtio_blk or ahci succeeds.


switch_root: bad newroot /newroot

Root Cause: switch_root has strict POSIX safety checks:

/newroot must be an active mount point (not just a plain directory).
The target binary (/newroot/sbin/init) must exist and have executable permissions.
The current root must be a tmpfs or ramfs (which initramfs is).

Remedy: Ensure your init script successfully mounts the root filesystem before invoking switch_root.

title: Troubleshooting: Boot Chain Failures
text:
Debugging Flags for the Bootloader
When booting, press e in GRUB to edit the kernel command line: - Remove quiet and splash. - Add rd.debug (for dracut) or debug. - Add init=/bin/sh to bypass all init systems and boot directly into a root shell.

title: A Brief History of Init Systems
text:
A Brief History of Init Systems
When the Linux kernel completes initialization, it calls run_init_process("/sbin/init"). As Process ID 1, this executable is the ancestor of every userspace process on the machine.
Over the past four decades, operating system initialization has evolved across four distinct eras.

title: A Brief History of Init Systems
text:
Era 1: Classic System V Init (SysVinit)
Originally developed for AT&T UNIX System V, sysvinit organized system states into numeric runlevels: - 0: Halt - 1 / S: Single-user rescue mode - 3: Multi-user text mode with networking - 5: Multi-user graphical mode with X11 - 6: Reboot
Services were managed by numbered shell script symlinks in /etc/rc<runlevel>.d/ pointing to /etc/init.d/:
/etc/rc3.d/S10network -> /etc/init.d/network
/etc/rc3.d/S20ssh     -> /etc/init.d/ssh
/etc/rc3.d/S30cron    -> /etc/init.d/cron
SysVinit executed these scripts sequentially in alphabetical order. Because each shell script had to fork multiple subshells (grep, sed, awk, cat), boot times were slow. Tracking processes required brittle /var/run/*.pid files; if a daemon double-forked and crashed, the init system had no way of knowing whether the process was alive.

title: A Brief History of Init Systems
section: The Push for Concurrency and Containment
text:
The Push for Concurrency and Containment
Modern machines feature dozens of CPU cores and hot-pluggable USB and NVMe devices. An init system cannot assume hardware is static at power-on. Modern systems require: 1. Parallel Activation: Booting services concurrently across available CPU cores. 2. Reliable Process Containment: Using Linux cgroups to track every child process spawned by a service, preventing orphaned daemons. 3. Socket and Bus Activation: Delaying daemon startup until a connection arrives on a UNIX socket or D-Bus endpoint.

title: Deep Dive: systemd Targets, Units, and Dependencies
text:
Deep Dive: systemd Targets, Units, and Dependencies
Created by Lennart Poettering and Kay Sievers, systemd is the dominant init system and system configuration suite across enterprise Linux distributions.

title: Deep Dive: systemd Targets, Units, and Dependencies
text:
Units: Declarative State Configurations
Unlike SysVinit scripts, systemd uses declarative INI-style unit files placed in /usr/lib/systemd/system/ (vendor defaults) and /etc/systemd/system/ (admin overrides):
# /etc/systemd/system/sshd.service
[Unit]
Description=OpenSSH Server Daemon
Documentation=man:sshd(8)
After=network.target auditd.service
ConditionPathExists=!/etc/ssh/sshd_not_to_be_run

[Service]
Type=notify
ExecStart=/usr/sbin/sshd -D $SSHD_OPTS
ExecReload=/bin/kill -HUP $MAINPID
KillMode=process
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=42s

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

title: Deep Dive: systemd Targets, Units, and Dependencies
text:
Understanding Dependency Directives

Requires=: Hard dependency. If unit B is listed in unit A’s Requires=, starting A will start B. If B fails to activate, A will not start.
Wants=: Soft dependency. systemd attempts to start B when A starts, but failure of B does not prevent A from running.
After= / Before=: Ordering only, not dependency. Declares the sequence of activation without implying whether the unit must be started.
BindsTo=: Strongest dependency. If unit B stops or crashes, unit A is immediately shut down.

title: Deep Dive: systemd Targets, Units, and Dependencies
text:
Targets: Replacing Runlevels
systemd replaces numeric runlevels with targets (.target units), which group sets of services: - emergency.target: Minimal single-process shell with root mounted read-only. - rescue.target: Single-user mode with essential filesystems mounted. - multi-user.target: Standard text-mode multi-user system (corresponds to SysV runlevel 3). - graphical.target: Multi-user system with display manager and GUI (corresponds to SysV runlevel 5).

title: Deep Dive: systemd Targets, Units, and Dependencies
text:
Socket Activation
In socket activation, systemd creates and listens on a network port or UNIX socket (.socket unit) before the application starts. When the first client connects, systemd passes the open file descriptor to the newly spawned daemon (.service unit). This eliminates ordering dependencies: clients can connect to dbus or sshd while they are still loading into memory without experiencing dropped connections.

title: OpenRC: Dependency-Based Service Management
text:
OpenRC: Dependency-Based Service Management
Developed originally by the Gentoo Linux project and adopted by Alpine Linux, OpenRC is a dependency-based service manager that works seamlessly alongside classic init systems (such as sysvinit or BusyBox init).

title: OpenRC: Dependency-Based Service Management
section: Why OpenRC Appeals to Distro Builders
text:
Why OpenRC Appeals to Distro Builders

Lightweight & Portable: OpenRC is written in clean C99 and standard POSIX shell. It does not require glibc, compiling cleanly on musl-libc and BSD systems.
Transparent Shell Scripts: Unlike systemd’s monolithic binary code, OpenRC services are standard shell scripts located in /etc/init.d/, making debugging and introspection straightforward.
Named Runlevels: Instead of arbitrary numbers, OpenRC uses human-readable runlevels: sysinit, boot, default, nonetwork, and custom user runlevels.

title: OpenRC: Dependency-Based Service Management
text:
Writing an OpenRC Service Script
OpenRC scripts define dependencies declaratively inside a depend() function:
#!/sbin/openrc-run
# /etc/init.d/sshd

description="OpenSSH Secure Shell Server"
command="/usr/sbin/sshd"
command_args="-D"
pidfile="/run/sshd.pid"

depend() {
    need net
    use logger dns
    after firewall
}

Dependency Semantics:

need: Mandatory dependency. The service will refuse to start if the required dependency is not available.
use: Optional dependency. If present in the runlevel, it will start first; if absent, it is ignored.
provide: Declares a virtual service capability. For example, both dhcpcd and static-ip provide net. Services requiring network connectivity simply state need net.

title: OpenRC: Dependency-Based Service Management
text:
Managing Services and Runlevels
# Add sshd to start automatically at boot:
# rc-update add sshd default

# Remove a service from startup:
# rc-update del apache2 default

# Start, stop, or query status:
# rc-service sshd start
# rc-service sshd status

# List all services and their assigned runlevels:
# rc-status

title: s6 and runit: The Minimalist Approach
text:
s6 and runit: The Minimalist Approach
In the lineage of Daniel J. Bernstein’s daemontools, runit and s6 represent the pinnacle of process supervision based strictly on the UNIX philosophy: write small programs that do one thing well, and compose them together.

title: s6 and runit: The Minimalist Approach
text:
The Supervision Tree Model
In traditional init systems, daemons fork into the background and detach from their parent. If the daemon crashes, the init system does not know about it.
In supervision systems: - Daemons are forbidden to fork or background themselves (-D or foreground mode). - A dedicated lightweight supervisor process (s6-supervise or runsv) runs as the direct parent of the daemon. - The supervisor monitors the daemon via waitpid(). If the daemon crashes, the supervisor restarts it instantly in milliseconds. - Standard output and error streams are piped directly into a dedicated logging daemon (s6-log or svlogd) running with unprivileged credentials, preventing disk exhaustion via automatic rotation.

title: s6 and runit: The Minimalist Approach
text:
runit: Pure Simplicity (Void Linux)
runit operates via a three-stage directory lifecycle: - Stage 1 (/etc/runit/1): One-time system initialization (mounts, hostname, clock). - Stage 2 (/etc/runit/2): Launches the service directory (/var/service). - Stage 3 (/etc/runit/3): Clean system shutdown, unmounting storage and halting.
A service is simply a directory containing an executable run script:
#!/bin/sh
# /etc/sv/sshd/run
exec /usr/sbin/sshd -D
Enabling a service is accomplished by creating a symbolic link:
# ln -s /etc/sv/sshd /var/service/
The runsvdir daemon notices the new symlink within 5 seconds and launches the supervisor automatically.

title: s6 and runit: The Minimalist Approach
text:
s6: High-Assurance Supervision
Developed by Laurent Bercot (Skaaware), s6 is an industrial-strength supervision suite designed to eliminate race conditions completely: - Provides transactional notifications using FIFOs and readiness events (s6-notifyoncheck). - Fully supports cgroup management and notification protocols without requiring a monolithic binary. - Exceptionally tiny footprint: entire supervision stack fits in under 200 KB of RAM.

title: BusyBox Init for Bare-Minimum Systems
text:
BusyBox Init for Bare-Minimum Systems
If your distribution targets micro-appliances, recovery shells, or embedded systems with strict storage limitations (e.g., less than 16 MB of total storage), BusyBox Init provides a complete PID 1 solution compiled directly into the BusyBox binary.

title: BusyBox Init for Bare-Minimum Systems
text:
The /etc/inittab Configuration
BusyBox init does not use traditional SysV runlevels (0-6). Instead, it reads /etc/inittab where each line follows the format:
<id>::<action>:<process>

<id>: The controlling tty device (e.g., tty1, ttyS0), or empty for non-interactive processes.
<action>:

sysinit: Executed first during system startup before anything else.
wait: Executed and waited on before continuing.
once: Started once in the background without waiting.
respawn: Restarted immediately if it ever terminates (ideal for shells and login prompts).
shutdown: Executed when the system is halted or rebooted.
ctrlaltdel: Executed when the user presses Ctrl+Alt+Del on the keyboard.

title: BusyBox Init for Bare-Minimum Systems
text:
A Production Bare-Minimum /etc/inittab
# /etc/inittab — Minimal BYOL Appliance Init
# 1. System initialization script
::sysinit:/etc/init.d/rcS

# 2. Virtual console login shells (automatically restarted if logged out)
tty1::respawn:/sbin/getty 38400 tty1
tty2::respawn:/sbin/getty 38400 tty2

# 3. Serial console (for headless QEMU or cloud instances)
ttyS0::respawn:/sbin/getty -L ttyS0 115200 vt100

# 4. Keyboard reboot hook
::ctrlaltdel:/sbin/reboot

# 5. Shutdown script (unmounting disks cleanly)
::shutdown:/etc/init.d/rcK

title: BusyBox Init for Bare-Minimum Systems
text:
The Companion Initialization Script (/etc/init.d/rcS)
#!/bin/sh
# /etc/init.d/rcS — Early boot mounts and setup
echo "[rcS] Initializing system pseudo-filesystems..."
mount -t proc none /proc
mount -t sysfs none /sys
mount -t devtmpfs none /dev

# Populate device nodes
echo "[rcS] Starting mdev..."
echo /sbin/mdev > /proc/sys/kernel/hotplug
mdev -s

# Set hostname and bring up loopback network
hostname -F /etc/hostname
ifconfig lo 127.0.0.1 up
With this configuration, your operating system boots in less than 200 milliseconds and consumes less than 4 megabytes of total RAM!

title: Case Study: Alpine’s OpenRC vs. Debian’s systemd
text:
Case Study: Alpine’s OpenRC vs. Debian’s systemd
The choice of init system represents a major fork in distribution philosophy. Comparing Debian’s adoption of systemd with Alpine’s retention of OpenRC illustrates the trade-offs of modern systems design.

title: Case Study: Alpine’s OpenRC vs. Debian’s systemd
text:
Debian: The Integrated Platform
Debian adopted systemd because modern desktop environments and enterprise infrastructure require tight coupling: - systemd-logind: Automatically manages seat assignment, virtual console switching, and device node ACL permissions (e.g., granting non-root users access to GPU DRM nodes and audio servers when they log into a graphical seat). - Structured Journaling: Logs capture kernel metadata, boot timestamps, process UIDs, and cgroup identifiers, preventing unprivileged log injection. - Declarative Isolation: Setting ProtectSystem=strict, NoNewPrivileges=true, and PrivateTmp=yes directly in a service file sandboxes daemons without writing custom AppArmor or SELinux profiles.

title: Case Study: Alpine’s OpenRC vs. Debian’s systemd
section: Alpine: The Lean Container & Appliance Champion
text:
Alpine: The Lean Container & Appliance Champion
Alpine retained OpenRC because its primary target is lightweight virtual appliances, container hosts, and routers: - Containers running on Docker or Kubernetes do not need an init system that manages hardware power-off states, backlight brightness, or Bluetooth adapters. - In container environments, systemd’s requirement to run with full cgroup permissions and host D-Bus sockets creates significant container breakout surface. - OpenRC scripts are completely transparent: an engineer can inspect /etc/init.d/chrony and understand every step of daemon execution using standard shell knowledge.

title: Case Study: Alpine’s OpenRC vs. Debian’s systemd
text:
Decision Matrix for BYOL Builders

If your custom distribution features GNOME, KDE Plasma, complex container runtimes, or enterprise services: integrate systemd.
If your distribution is a minimal server, musl-based container base, network router, or i3/sway desktop: integrate OpenRC or runit.

title: Troubleshooting: Init System Failures
text:
Troubleshooting: Init System Failures
When Process ID 1 fails during boot, the operating system halts or hangs indefinitely. Because userspace logging daemons have not started yet, troubleshooting init failures requires specific diagnostic techniques.

title: Troubleshooting: Init System Failures
text:
Diagnostic 1: The Direct Shell Bypass (init=/bin/sh)
If PID 1 crashes, refuses to start, or locks you out with an unconfigured root password, reboot the machine and append the following parameter to the kernel command line in your bootloader:
init=/bin/sh
This bypasses systemd, OpenRC, and /sbin/init entirely. The Linux kernel mounts the root filesystem (often read-only) and immediately spawns a root /bin/sh shell.
Once in the shell:
# Remount the root filesystem read-write:
# mount -o remount,rw /

# Verify executable permissions and dynamic linking on the real init:
# ldd /sbin/init
# /sbin/init --version

title: Troubleshooting: Init System Failures
text:
Diagnostic 2: Diagnosing systemd Boot Freezes
If systemd hangs during boot: 1. Enable Systemd Debug Logging: Add to the kernel command line: text    systemd.log_level=debug systemd.log_target=kmsg systemd.debug_shell=1 - systemd.debug_shell=1: Spawns a root shell on tty9 (Ctrl+Alt+F9) automatically, allowing you to log in even if the graphical login manager freezes. 2. Inspect Slow Units: Once booted, analyze boot bottlenecks using: ```bash $ systemd-analyze Startup finished in 1.203s (kernel) + 2.140s (userspace) = 3.343s
$ systemd-analyze blame | head -n 10 3. **Generate a Dependency Chart:** Visualize cyclic dependencies or long activation paths:bash $ systemd-analyze plot > boot-timeline.svg ```

title: Troubleshooting: Init System Failures
text:
Diagnostic 3: OpenRC Dependency Loops
In OpenRC, if two services depend on each other (e.g., service A needs B, and service B needs A), OpenRC will detect a cyclic dependency in its Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) and abort:
 * rc: Service 'sshd' has a dependency loop with 'network'
Remedy: 1. Boot into single-user mode: add single or init=/bin/sh to kernel parameters. 2. Check the dependency trees of both services in /etc/init.d/. 3. Change one of the hard need statements to a soft use or after directive.

title: Packaging Formats Compared: .deb, .rpm, .pkg.tar.zst, .apk
text:
Packaging Formats Compared: .deb, .rpm, .pkg.tar.zst, .apk
The package format is the fundamental currency of a distribution. Stripped of branding, a package is simply an archive containing: 1. The compiled files to be installed into the filesystem (/usr/bin, /usr/lib, /etc). 2. Declarative metadata (package name, version, architecture, license, dependencies). 3. Optional maintainer hook scripts (pre-install, post-install, pre-removal, post-removal).

title: Packaging Formats Compared: .deb, .rpm, .pkg.tar.zst, .apk
text:
Deconstructing Debian’s .deb Format
Debian .deb packages use the standard UNIX ar archive utility, ensuring they can be inspected on any UNIX system without special tools:
# Extracting a .deb package manually using standard binutils:
$ ar -x curl_7.88.1-10_amd64.deb
$ ls -l
-rw-r--r-- 1 user user      4 debian-binary
-rw-r--r-- 1 user user   2144 control.tar.xz
-rw-r--r-- 1 user user 289412 data.tar.xz

# Inspecting the control metadata:
$ tar -xf control.tar.xz
$ cat control
Package: curl
Version: 7.88.1-10
Architecture: amd64
Maintainer: Debian curl team
Depends: libc6 (>= 2.34), libcurl4 (= 7.88.1-10), zlib1g (>= 1:1.1.4)
Description: command line tool for transferring data with URL syntax

title: Packaging Formats Compared: .deb, .rpm, .pkg.tar.zst, .apk
text:
Deconstructing Arch Linux’s .pkg.tar.zst
Arch Linux packages prioritize raw speed and simplicity. Instead of nesting archives, an Arch package is a single tar archive compressed using Facebook’s high-speed Zstandard (zstd) algorithm:
# Decompressing and inspecting an Arch package:
$ tar --zstd -tf ripgrep-14.1.0-1-x86_64.pkg.tar.zst
.PKGINFO
.BUILDINFO
.MTREE
usr/
usr/bin/
usr/bin/rg
usr/share/man/man1/rg.1.gz
Because .pkg.tar.zst contains the actual filesystem tree directly at the root of the archive, package installation is as fast as unpacking a tarball directly into /!

title: Packaging Formats Compared: .deb, .rpm, .pkg.tar.zst, .apk
text:
Deconstructing Alpine’s .apk Format
